q: בן 81, עם סרטן ריאות מתקדם, מאושפז במחלקה האונקולוגית לקבלת טיפולים כימותרפיים והקרנות. המטופל תשוש, מדווח על תאבון ירוד ואוכל מעט. בנוסף סובל מתופעות לוואי מהטיפולים שמקבל. מהי הגישה לגבי טיפולים תומכים במטופל זה?
o: טיפול פליאטיבי משפר את איכות החיים של המטופל, אבל לא את ההישרדות הכללית
לתשישות המאפיינת מטופלים אונקולוגיים רבים אין טיפול פרמקולוגי
הטיפול בבחילות ניתן רק במידה ויש סימפטומים ולא כטיפול מונע
אם למטופל יש דיכאון סביר לתת טיפול ב- MIRTAZAPINE (MIRO)
explanation:
**Mirtazapine** is a reasonable option when an older cancer patient has depression: the source describes benefits for mood, appetite and sleep in patients with cancer (p. 1392).

**A. Palliative care improves quality of life but not overall survival.** Wrong, studies of early palliative care also describe improved survival, so a blanket denial of survival benefit is incorrect (pp. 1047, 1392).
**B. There is no pharmacologic treatment for cancer-related fatigue.** Wrong, pharmacologic approaches are described, including stimulants and corticosteroids; the categorical claim is unsupported (p. 1392).
**C. Antiemetic treatment is given only after symptoms appear, never prophylactically.** Wrong, the source describes routine antiemetic use and a study administering drugs before chemotherapy; symptoms need not first develop (p. 1391).
**D. If the patient has depression, mirtazapine is reasonable.** Correct, potential benefits for mood, appetite and sleep make it reasonable to consider if depression is present in this setting (p. 1392).
Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1047, 1391-1392.

q: בן 86, מאובחן עם דמנציה מתקדמת, מאושפז במחלקה לסיעוד מורכב עקב פצעי לחץ בדרגה 4 בעכוז ובעקב, מוגדר כנוטה למות, פיתח דלקת ריאות מאספירציה, מה נכון לגבי הטיפול?
o: טיפול אנטיביוטי משפר הישרדות אך לא נוחות
המטופל מוגדר כנוטה למות אין לתת טיפול אנטיביוטי
יש להפסיק האכלה פומית ולהכניס זונדה למתן אוכל ותרופות
יש להגדיר את המטופל כנוטה למות במצב סופי ולהתחיל סדציה פליאטיבית
explanation:
For aspiration pneumonia in advanced dementia, **antibiotics are associated with improved survival but not improved comfort**. More aggressive treatment, particularly intravenous therapy and hospitalization, is associated with greater discomfort; decisions should reflect the goals of care (Hazzard 8e, p. 1048).

**A. Antibiotics improve survival but not comfort.** Correct, this is the officially accepted option and the association described in the source. It does not mean antibiotics are obligatory in every case; treatment depends on care goals (p. 1048).
**B. Antibiotics must not be given because the patient is defined as dying.** Wrong, that designation does not automatically prohibit antibiotics. Establish the patient's wishes, condition, and capacity, and reconsider treatment when these change (Dying Patient Law, sections 9, 12; Hazzard, p. 1048).
**C. Stop oral feeding and insert a nasogastric tube for food and medicines.** Wrong, automatic tube placement is not justified. The Israeli recommendations prefer oral food and fluids and individualized decisions about the feeding route (committee recommendations, p. 5).
**D. Define the patient as being in the final stage of dying and begin palliative sedation.** Wrong, final-stage designation has separate criteria involving failure of vital systems and a very short life expectancy; pneumonia alone does not establish it. Palliative sedation is a last resort for refractory, intolerable distress, which is not described here (Dying Patient Law, section 8(b); Hazzard, p. 1105).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1048, 1105; Israeli Dying Patient Law, sections 8(b), 9, 12; Israeli committee recommendations on feeding patients with dementia, p. 5.

q: בת 89 סובלת מסרטן ריאות גרורתי, תוחלת חיים משוערת של מספר חודשים. מטופלת בהוספיס בית. מה הגישה הנכונה לאיזון סוכרת במצבה?
o: עדיפות לשימוש במעכבי SGLT2 להשגת המוגלובין A1C 7-7.5%
הפסקת טיפול תרופתי לסוכרת והפסקת מעקב בדיקות דם
שחרור ההגבלות התזונתיות
איזון סוכר בצום בערכים בין 100 ל- 130
explanation:
Official answer: ג

With terminal illness and a prognosis of months, diabetes care shifts toward **comfort and quality of life**. Relaxing dietary restrictions and simplifying the regimen are part of that adjustment, while avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia (p. 1586).

**A. Prefer SGLT2 inhibitors to achieve HbA1c 7–7.5%.** Wrong, intensification to this tight target is not the goal in the final months; care should reduce treatment burden and symptoms (p. 1586).
**B. Stop all diabetes medication and blood-test monitoring.** Wrong, blanket cessation is not appropriate solely because prognosis is measured in months. Some patients still need treatment and monitoring to prevent thirst, dehydration and other hyperglycemic symptoms (p. 1586).
**C. Relax dietary restrictions.** Correct, the table explicitly recommends this in advanced disease with a prognosis of months, particularly when oral intake is poor, to fit comfort and eating ability (Table 99-16, p. 1586).
**D. Target fasting glucose of 100–130.** Wrong, this is tighter than the end-of-life goals presented. The source gives a general range of 108–270 mg/dL, individualized to clinical condition and symptom avoidance (p. 1586).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1586.

q: בן 78, עם סרטן ערמונית מתקדם גרורתי, הוגדר כסופני (בשבועיים האחרונים לחייו). סוכם עם בני משפחתו על טיפול תומך בלבד. באשפוז נכנס לדליריום היפראקטיבי עם סימני אי-שקט פסיכומוטורי. טיפול ב- HALOPERIDOL לא עזר. מה הגישה לגבי טיפול בבנזודאזפינים במצב זה?
o: יש להימנע מטיפול בבנזודאזפינים מאחר שמחמירים דליריום
מומלץ שימוש בתרופות מסוג בנזודאזפינים ארוכי טווח כגון DIAZEPAM
יש להימנע ככל הניתן ממתן בזריקות ולהתמקד במתן פומי
מומלץ טיפול בבנזודיאזפינים קצרי טווח כגון MIDAZOLAM עם אפשרות טיטרציה
explanation:
In a dying patient with hyperactive delirium unresponsive to haloperidol, the goal is **relief of distress**, not necessarily preservation of alertness. When end-of-life sedation is indicated, the source recommends a short-acting agent that can be titrated to effect and goals of care; it describes oral, intravenous or subcutaneous lorazepam according to the patient's needs (p. 890).

**A. Avoid benzodiazepines because they worsen delirium.** Wrong, despite the risk of worsening confusion, sedation may be needed for severe agitation at the end of life in accordance with goals of care. Blanket avoidance misses this exception (p. 890).
**B. Use long-acting benzodiazepines such as diazepam.** Wrong, long duration does not match the preference for a short-acting agent whose effect can be adjusted (p. 890).
**C. Avoid injections whenever possible and focus on oral treatment.** Wrong, the source also describes intravenous or subcutaneous sedation and does not require an oral preference in every such case (p. 890).
**D. Use a short-acting benzodiazepine such as midazolam with titration.** Correct, officially accepted. The short-acting, titratable-agent principle is supported, but the book's named example is lorazepam; this page is not direct support for the specific midazolam recommendation (p. 890).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 890.

q: Must a patient stop curative treatment to receive palliative care?
o: Yes; palliative care generally begins after disease-directed therapy has been abandoned
Yes; curative treatment usually needs to be stopped before palliative care begins
No; palliative care is compatible with continued treatment aimed at cure
No; eligibility for palliative care depends on prior enrollment in hospice
explanation:
**Palliative care** relieves the symptoms, pain and stress of serious illness. This purpose is compatible with treatment aimed at cure: it “can be provided together with curative treatment.” Hospice is a specialized form for patients with limited life expectancy, rather than a prerequisite for all palliative care (p. 1045).

**A. Yes; palliative care generally begins after disease-directed therapy has been abandoned.** Wrong, waiting until disease-directed treatment is abandoned imposes a sequence the source does not require; palliative care and curative treatment can be provided together (p. 1045).
**B. Yes; curative treatment usually needs to be stopped before palliative care begins.** Wrong, stopping curative treatment is not a prerequisite for addressing symptoms and suffering alongside it (p. 1045).
**C. No; palliative care is compatible with continued treatment aimed at cure.** Correct, care for symptoms, pain and stress can accompany treatment directed at curing the serious illness (p. 1045).
**D. No; eligibility for palliative care depends on prior enrollment in hospice.** Wrong, hospice is a specialized form for limited life expectancy, whereas palliative care is appropriate at any stage of serious illness (p. 1045).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, p. 1045.
ref: Hazzard 8e Ch 67 · p1045

o: The hospice director alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
An LCD automatically certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
The attending physician and hospice director certify terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
The attending physician alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course
explanation:

D. The attending physician alone certifies terminal illness and prognosis under 6 months if the disease runs its usual and expected course: The described certification involves both physicians (p1046).

q: Does absence of a single terminal disease automatically exclude a frail patient from hospice?
o: No; prognosis rests on the severity and irreversibility of frailty and multimorbidity
No; certification of a terminal prognosis is optional when frailty is present
Yes; the principal-diagnosis billing restriction generally makes frail patients ineligible
Yes; frailty with multimorbidity is insufficient grounds for a terminal prognosis
explanation:
**Hospice eligibility** depends on a certified terminal prognosis, not on having one named terminal disease. In the US Medicare framework described here, the severity and irreversibility of frailty together with multimorbidity inform prognosis; the principal-diagnosis billing restriction does not itself exclude a frail patient (p. 1049). “Patients with frailty and multimorbidity may still be eligible for hospice even if they do not have a single terminal illness.” (p. 1049).

**A. No; prognosis rests on the severity and irreversibility of frailty and multimorbidity.** Correct, the combined severity and irreversibility inform a prognosis that the attending physician and hospice medical director must certify as less than six months (p. 1049).
**B. No; certification of a terminal prognosis is optional when frailty is present.** Wrong, frailty does not waive the requirement for physician certification of terminal illness and the required prognosis (p. 1049).
**C. Yes; the principal-diagnosis billing restriction generally makes frail patients ineligible.** Wrong, the source distinguishes the billing restriction from eligibility for the hospice benefit; it does not automatically exclude frail patients (p. 1049).
**D. Yes; frailty with multimorbidity is insufficient grounds for a terminal prognosis.** Wrong, the source explicitly permits a prognosis based on frailty and multimorbidity when their severity and irreversibility support it (p. 1049).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, p. 1049.

q: Why compare prognosis with time to benefit?
o: Short life expectancy tends to bring forward the benefit of preventive interventions
Preventive interventions generally spare frail patients the immediate harms associated with treatment
Life expectancy sometimes ends before preventive benefit develops, exposing patients to immediate harms
Prognosis is relevant to hospice selection but generally irrelevant to preventive treatment
explanation:
**Time to benefit** matters because preventive interventions may cause harm before their benefits accrue. A frail patient whose life expectancy is shorter than that interval is exposed to immediate harms without living long enough to receive the preventive benefit; prognosis therefore informs preventive decisions as well as hospice eligibility (p. 1050). The source describes “potential immediate harms of these preventative interventions without the possibility of receiving the benefits.” (p. 1050).

**A. Short life expectancy tends to bring forward the benefit of preventive interventions.** Wrong, a short prognosis does not shorten the intervention’s time to benefit. Benefits may take years to accrue despite the patient’s shorter remaining life (p. 1050).
**B. Preventive interventions generally spare frail patients the immediate harms associated with treatment.** Wrong, the source warns of potential immediate harms in frail patients whose life expectancy is shorter than the benefit horizon (p. 1050).
**C. Life expectancy sometimes ends before preventive benefit develops, exposing patients to immediate harms.** Correct, this captures the mismatch between remaining life expectancy and delayed benefit: harms occur during treatment even when the future benefit will not be reached (p. 1050).
**D. Prognosis is relevant to hospice selection but generally irrelevant to preventive treatment.** Wrong, the source explicitly uses prognosis to target interventions to people likely to live long enough to benefit; its role extends beyond hospice (p. 1050).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, p. 1050.
